lessons.title: Word Roots and Meaning
lessons.concept: Many English words are built from roots (core meaning units), often from Latin or Greek origins. Recognizing common roots can help infer meanings of unfamiliar words. For example, 'dict' relates to saying/speaking (predict, dictionary), and 'port' relates to carrying (transport, portable).
lessons.formula: Strategy: break word into parts (prefix + root + suffix) -> infer meaning from known parts -> confirm with context.
lessons.worked_example: 'Inspect' can be seen as in- (into) + spect (look) -> to look into/examine. 'Export' = ex- (out) + port (carry) -> carry out/send out.
mistakes: Assuming every word's meaning is fully determined by parts (etymology can shift)

lessons.title: Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.concept: Prefixes modify meaning at the beginning of a word (e.g., un- = not, re- = again, pre- = before). Suffixes attach at the end and can change meaning or word form/part of speech (e.g., -ful = full of, -less = without, -tion = noun form of action).
lessons.formula: Common prefixes: un-/in-/im-/non- (negation), re- (again), pre- (before), mis- (wrongly). Common suffixes: -able/-ible (can be), -er/-or (doer), -ness (state/quality).
lessons.worked_example: 'Unhappy' = un (not) + happy. 'Readable' = read + able (can be read). 'Kindness' = kind + ness (quality of being kind).
mistakes: Misreading prefix meaning (e.g., 'incredible' historically means hard to believe, though usage varies)
Assuming suffix always keeps same meaning across all words
Ignoring spelling changes when affixes are added

lessons.title: Context Clues and Word Usage
lessons.concept: Context clues in a sentence help determine the meaning of an unfamiliar word. Clues may include definitions, synonyms/antonyms nearby, examples, or overall tone. Vocabulary building also involves understanding collocations and choosing words that fit meaning and usage.
lessons.formula: Use context: look for signal words (but/however for contrast, such as/for example for examples), surrounding meaning, and sentence logic.
lessons.worked_example: Sentence: 'The arid region received almost no rain for months.' Context 'almost no rain' suggests 'arid' means dry.
mistakes: Choosing a dictionary meaning that doesn't fit context
